description: We're Somehow Alive, a 6-member team at our first hackathon (Giza, Egypt). We built a browser game for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge: a rookie astronaut must keep a Mars base alive while the expert crew is away, learning real NASA science one decision at a time.
summary: Somehow Alive is a browser game for children aged 7–12 in which a rookie astronaut, Freddy, must keep a Mars base alive while the expert crew is away. It turns the challenge's trade-offs into decisions kids can feel: power, life support, food production and radiation safety. Players water the greenhouse with a limited tank, wipe dust off solar panels, plan energy before the freezing night and photograph a real blue Martian sunset. After each task, the robot ORBI explains the science with a NASA source, and a free time-rewind replaces Game Over so failing becomes the lesson. It matters because kids in Egypt usually meet space science as facts to memorize, in a language that isn't theirs. Our game is Arabic-first with English, runs on any phone with no install, and teaches why astronauts make the choices they make.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Space science usually reaches kids as facts to memorize. They never feel why astronauts exercise for hours, guard every drop of water, or hide from the Sun, and in Egypt most of this content isn't even in their language.

WHAT IT DOES

Somehow Alive is a browser game where the player is Freddy, a rookie astronaut who must keep a Mars base alive while the expert crew drives away to collect underground ice. The base is modeled on NASA's 3D-printed Mars Dune Alpha habitat: a corridor, greenhouse, gym, control room, kitchen, crew quarters and a rover garage. Rooms the story doesn't need yet are locked for future days.

Sol 1 (playable now):

• Animated comic intro with Arabic voice-over sets up the crew, the ice mission and Freddy.

• Greenhouse: water the plants with a limited tank (food production vs. water supply).

• Solar panel repair: wipe red Mars dust off the panels to restore power.

• Night: the base runs on solar panels and batteries, so energy used by day decides whether the lights stay on at night.

• Blue sunset selfie: recreate the real blue Martian sunset photographed by Curiosity.

After each task, ORBI the robot explains the real science in two short sentences, with its NASA source.

HOW IT WORKS

Three crew rules in priority order (1. stay safe, 2. keep the base alive, 3. do the mission) turn every choice into a learnable trade-off between power, life support, food and radiation safety. Mistakes have visible consequences, like a blackout where you walk the base by flashlight. ORBI then rewinds the day and explains why. No Game Over: failing is the lesson.

BENEFITS & IMPACT

Kids learn why astronauts do what they do, and connect it to Earth: gravity and exercise, recycling water, solar storms and GPS, dust on Egypt's own Benban solar park. A 12–15 minute experience for children aged 7–12, usable at home, in schools and in science clubs across the Arabic-speaking world.

COMING NEXT

• Sol 2, Solar Storm: based on the real May 20, 2024 event measured by Curiosity. Earth's reply arrives after the peak, so the player must decide alone to shelter behind the base's water tanks.

• Sol 3, Dust Storm: inspired by Opportunity in 2018. The panels go dark, and the power saved the night before keeps the beacon on to guide the crew home.

• A gym task, a delayed daily report to Earth, a teacher worksheet and a Junior Astronaut certificate.

TOOLS

Godot 4 (GDScript) exported to HTML5/WebAssembly for phones and laptops; pixel art; motion comic edited with FFmpeg and Python; website on Vercel (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) with live NASA DONKI space-weather data.

TEAM

Mohamed (story, science, presentation) · Omar (game development) · Khaled (website) · Asia (presentation, voice-over) · Miraj (game art, comic) · Maryam (illustration, storyboards)

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Science is delivered by a character, not a textbook: ORBI, a calm robot who speaks only when it matters. The story is a comic told with original voice acting, and the game's ambient sound is the real first recording of Mars from Perseverance. Failing is designed as the best teacher: a visible consequence, then a rewind with an explanation.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

• Age 7–12: short tasks (under 1 minute each), big buttons, two-sentence explanations.

• Access: runs in any browser on low-end phones, Arabic-first with English.

• Scientific validity: every number checked against NASA or ESA sources; we clearly separate real facts, gameplay simplifications and fiction.

• Honest scope: Sol 1 is fully playable; Sols 2–3 are designed and storyboarded.
